what_it_does: When a specialized chip (like a GPU or an AI accelerator — a chip purpose-built to run one class of computation very fast) is added to a computer system, it must communicate with the rest of the machine over a high-speed link called PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express), a standardized electrical bus that connects chips on a motherboard. The speed and structure of that link, and of the memory chips attached to the accelerator, can dramatically affect how fast the whole system runs — but designers rarely have good tools to explore these trade-offs before committing to silicon. This paper presents a simulation framework built on top of gem5, a widely used open-source computer architecture simulator, that lets engineers model different combinations of memory technologies (DDR4, DDR5, GDDR6, and HBM2 — each a different type of memory chip with different speed and cost profiles) and interconnect configurations. Using a matrix-multiplication workload typical of transformer AI models as a test case, the authors find that the best-tuned configuration reaches about 80% of the performance you would get if the memory were directly on the chip — a useful data point for future accelerator designs.
